sections.title: Geography
sections.text: New York City has five boroughs spread across islands and the mainland around one of the world's great natural harbours, where the Hudson River meets the Atlantic. Manhattan's street grid, planned in 1811, makes it easy to find your way: avenues run north–south and numbered streets run east–west.

sections.title: History
sections.text: This was the homeland of the Lenape people. The Dutch founded New Amsterdam here in the 1620s, and the English renamed it New York in 1664. The city was briefly the first capital of the United States. Between 1892 and 1954 about twelve million immigrants passed through nearby Ellis Island, and the city still carries their languages and foods.

sections.title: Culture
sections.text: Every neighbourhood feels like a different town, from Chinatown to Harlem to Little Italy. New York is a capital of theatre, music, art and food, and its bagels and thin-crust pizza are local institutions. The subway runs all day and all night.

etiquette: Tip about 18–20% in restaurants and bars. Staff rely on tips.
Walk briskly, keep to the right and don't stop in the middle of the pavement.
On the subway, let people get off before you get on.
Prices shown usually don't include sales tax. It's added at the till.

planned.name: Brooklyn Bridge
planned.blurb: A granite-towered suspension bridge, opened in 1883. You can walk across it for views of the Manhattan skyline.

timeline.text: Ancestors of the Lenape people fish and hunt along the rivers and shores of the great harbour.
Explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano sails into the harbour, the first known European visitor.
The Dutch colony of New Amsterdam grows on the southern tip of Manhattan.
The English take the colony and rename it New York.
George Washington is sworn in as the first US president at Federal Hall on Wall Street.
The Erie Canal opens, linking New York's harbour to the Great Lakes, and the city booms.
Work begins on the Brooklyn Bridge.
The Statue of Liberty is unveiled in New York Harbor.
Ellis Island opens. About twelve million immigrants will pass through it.
The Empire State Building opens and becomes the world's tallest building.
Crowds fill Times Square to celebrate the end of the Second World War.
New York faces a severe financial crisis and nearly runs out of money.
The restored Statue of Liberty celebrates its 100th birthday.
On 11 September terrorist attacks destroy the World Trade Center.
A city of more than eight million people, where hundreds of languages are spoken.
